title: Spec-Driven Testing for Agents With A Brain the Size of A Planet — Steven Willmott, SafeIntelligence
talk_summary: The speaker argues that agent validation should go beyond a static eval dataset to explicit role/task specs: rules, domain dictionaries, permissions, and robustness requirements. He recommends using those specs to drive security and robustness tests, kept implementation-independent and versioned so failures can be iterated automatically.

takeaways.what_they_do: Define each agent role with explicit rules, domain terms, rights/roles, and robustness requirements, then use that spec as the benchmark rather than only input/output examples.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need to go beyond the test set to have like task and role specific benchmarks that are for the agent itself.

takeaways.what_they_do: Vary agent inputs with typos, rephrasing, and stress cases to measure how stable task performance is under realistic change.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Rephrasing, how how stable under change are are the results?

takeaways.what_they_do: Use the agent's intended domain and tools to identify where it is most exposed, then test security around those allowed domains and actions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you know what an agent is trying to do, you know the edges of where it's vulnerable

takeaways.what_they_do: Keep integration, unit, and penetration tests independent of the orchestration framework so they can run against any implementation and be versioned like code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: keep those integration tests, all of the unit tests, and penetration tests and and run them independently.
There's this concept of an agent card which comes from the A to A spec.

takeaways.what_they_do: Automatically run the agent against the spec, collect results, and iterate on the gaps that appear.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run the agent automatically, get the results, and then start to iterate and try to fill the robustness gaps
